body:
The unfinished work of independence

India became independent on 15 August 1947, but independence did not immediately resolve the political, territorial and administrative challenges facing the country. Partition divided British India into India and Pakistan and caused widespread violence, migration and displacement. The new government had to rehabilitate refugees, integrate more than 500 princely states, establish democratic institutions and create a common constitutional framework for a population with enormous linguistic, religious and cultural diversity.

The integration of princely states was led by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, with V.P. Menon playing an important administrative role. Their integration into the Indian Union was an essential part of establishing India's territorial unity. However, the boundaries inherited from British provinces and princely states did not always correspond to linguistic, cultural or administrative identities.

Adoption of the Constitution and establishment of the Republic

The Constituent Assembly adopted the Constitution on 26 November 1949. It came into force on 26 January 1950, when India became a Republic. The date was selected in recognition of the observance of Independence Day on 26 January 1930 following the Congress's Purna Swaraj resolution of December 1929.

A Republic is a political system in which the head of State is not a hereditary monarch. India has an elected President as its constitutional head. The President is elected indirectly for a term of 5 years through an electoral college consisting of elected members of both Houses of Parliament and elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies, including those of Delhi and Puducherry. The election follows proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote and a secret ballot.

A Democracy is a system in which political authority ultimately rests with the people. Citizens exercise this authority through elections, representative institutions and constitutional rights. India adopted representative parliamentary democracy rather than direct democracy.

Republic and Democracy are different

Republic concerns how the head of State is selected. Democracy concerns the source and exercise of political power through the people. India is both a Republic and a Democracy.

The constitutional structure of the Union

Article 1 declares that India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States. The Constitution establishes a parliamentary system at the Union and State levels. The President is the constitutional head of the Union, while the Prime Minister leads the Council of Ministers responsible to the Lok Sabha. At the State level, the Governor is the constitutional head and the Chief Minister leads the Council of Ministers responsible to the Legislative Assembly.

The Constitution also establishes an independent judiciary and an independent Election Commission. These institutions help maintain constitutional government, protect rights and ensure that political authority is exercised according to law.

The original Preamble and its later amendment

The original Preamble described India as a Sovereign Democratic Republic. The Constitution (42nd Amendment) Act, 1976 inserted the words Socialist and Secular before Democratic and added Integrity to the expression Unity and Integrity of the Nation. The word Unity was already present in the original Preamble.

Prelims focus

  • Constitution adopted: 26 November 1949.
  • Constitution came into force: 26 January 1950.
  • Article 1 describes India as a Union of States.
  • The President is indirectly elected for a 5-year term.
  • The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 added Socialist, Secular and Integrity to the Preamble.
  • Trap: Socialist and Secular were not part of the original Preamble.

[Sources: GCERT, Social Science, Standard 9, Chapter 8, Framing of Constitution and its Features, pp. 56–63; NCERT, Politics in India Since Independence, Class XII, Chapter 1, Challenges of Nation Building; Constitution of India, Preamble, Articles 1 and 54–56; Constitution (42nd Amendment) Act, 1976. Online sources consulted 22 November 2026.]

title: From Independence to a Constitutional Republic

body:
A representative parliamentary system

The Constitution established a parliamentary system in which citizens elect representatives to legislatures and the executive remains accountable to the elected House. At the Union level, Parliament consists of the President, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha.

  • Lok Sabha: Members are directly elected by the people through territorial constituencies.
  • Rajya Sabha: Representatives of the States are elected indirectly by elected members of their Legislative Assemblies through proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote.
  • President: The constitutional head of the Union, elected indirectly by an electoral college.
  • State Legislative Assemblies: Members are directly elected by voters in their respective constituencies.

The Union Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha under Article 75(3). At the State level, the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly under Article 164(2). Therefore, a ministry must retain the confidence of the elected lower House to remain in office.

The Election Commission of India

Article 324 provides for the Election Commission of India (ECI). It has the constitutional responsibility for the superintendence, direction and control of elections to Parliament, State Legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President.

The Election Commission was established on 25 January 1950. Sukumar Sen was India's first Chief Election Commissioner. The constitutional independence of the Commission is important because elections must be conducted impartially, without improper interference by the government of the day.

Do not confuse the Election Commission of India with State Election Commissions. Elections to Panchayats are supervised by State Election Commissions under Article 243K, while elections to Municipalities are supervised under Article 243ZA. These local elections are not conducted by the Election Commission of India.

Universal adult franchise

Article 326 provides for elections to the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies on the basis of universal adult franchise. Every Indian citizen who has attained the age of 18 years on the qualifying date can be registered as an elector, subject to disqualifications under law.

When the Constitution commenced, the voting age was 21 years. The Constitution (61st Amendment) Act, 1988 reduced it to 18 years. This change came into effect on 28 March 1989.

Universal adult franchise from the beginning

India adopted adult suffrage without making the right to vote dependent on property ownership, income, educational qualifications, caste or sex. This was an important democratic choice in a newly independent country.

The first general election, 1951–52

India's first general election was conducted during 1951–52. It was a landmark because a newly independent country with widespread poverty, limited literacy and enormous geographical diversity successfully organised a nationwide democratic election.

Approximately 17.2 crore electors were eligible to participate under the voting age of 21 years applicable at that time. The election covered 489 Lok Sabha seats. It also involved elections to State Legislative Assemblies across the country.

Before the first elected Lok Sabha began functioning, the Constituent Assembly (Legislative) continued as the provisional Parliament from 26 January 1950. The first general election established an elected national legislature and gave practical effect to the constitutional commitment to representative democracy.

Prelims focus

  • Article 324: Election Commission of India.
  • Article 326: Elections based on adult suffrage.
  • Sukumar Sen: First Chief Election Commissioner.
  • First general elections: 1951–52; 489 Lok Sabha seats.
  • Voting age reduced from 21 to 18 by the 61st Amendment Act, 1988.
  • Trap: Panchayat and Municipal elections are conducted by State Election Commissions, not the Election Commission of India.

[Sources: GCERT, Social Science, Standard 9, Chapter 12, Indian Democracy, pp. 93–97; Constitution of India, Articles 75(3), 79–81, 164(2), 243K, 243ZA, 324 and 326; Constitution (61st Amendment) Act, 1988; Election Commission of India, Leap of Faith: Journey of Indian Elections, pp. 39–41; ECI Atlas of General Elections 1951–2024, p. 104. Consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Adult suffrage defines voters, the Election Commission administers elections, and elected Houses hold governments accountable.

title: Democratic Institutions and the First General Election

body:
Citizenship in a newly divided subcontinent

Citizenship is the legal status of full membership of a political community. It establishes a person's legal relationship with the State and determines eligibility for important constitutional rights and responsibilities.

India adopted the principle of single citizenship. A person is a citizen of India and does not hold a separate citizenship of an individual State. This supports a common political identity throughout the Union.

Partition created an immediate citizenship problem. People had migrated between India and Pakistan, sometimes more than once, and the new international boundary divided families and communities. Therefore, Part II of the Constitution, containing Articles 5–11, laid down who would be recognised as an Indian citizen when the Constitution commenced on 26 January 1950.

The constitutional provisions: Articles 5–11

ArticleCategoryMain provision
5Domicile in IndiaRequired domicile in India plus one of these conditions: birth in India, either parent born in India, or ordinary residence in India for at least 5 years immediately before commencement.
6Migration from Pakistan to IndiaRequired the migrant, either parent or any grandparent to have been born in India as defined in the Government of India Act, 1935 (as originally enacted). Those arriving before 19 July 1948 had to be ordinarily resident since migration. Those arriving on or after that date required registration by an officer appointed by the Government of the Dominion of India, on an application made before commencement, with at least 6 months of residence immediately before applying.
7Migration from India to PakistanPersons who migrated to Pakistan after 1 March 1947 were generally excluded, subject to an exception for those returning to India under a permit for resettlement or permanent return.
8Persons of Indian origin abroadPersons who, or whose parent or grandparent, were born in India as defined in the Government of India Act, 1935 (as originally enacted), and ordinarily resided outside India as so defined, could become citizens through registration by an Indian diplomatic or consular representative.
9Foreign citizenshipA person who voluntarily acquired citizenship of a foreign State was not a citizen under Articles 5, 6 or 8.
10Continuance of citizenshipPersons recognised as citizens under the preceding provisions continued as citizens, subject to laws made by Parliament.
11Parliament's authorityParliament received the power to make laws concerning acquisition, termination and other matters relating to citizenship.

Understanding the migration provisions

Article 5 dealt with people who had a domicile in India at the commencement of the Constitution. Domicile refers to a person's permanent legal home, not merely a temporary stay in a place.

Article 6 dealt with migration from territories that became part of Pakistan into India. It distinguished migrants who arrived before and after 19 July 1948. The later category had to satisfy a registration requirement, including 6 months of residence immediately before applying.

Article 7 addressed the opposite movement. A person who migrated from India to Pakistan after 1 March 1947 was generally not treated as an Indian citizen. However, a person who subsequently returned under a permit for resettlement or permanent return was deemed under Article 6(b) to have migrated after 19 July 1948 and required registration on an application made before commencement, with at least 6 months of residence immediately before applying.

Article 8 addressed persons of Indian origin who were living outside India. Article 9 dealt with voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship. Articles 10 and 11 established the continuation of citizenship and Parliament's authority to regulate it through legislation.

Constitutional citizenship and the Citizenship Act, 1955

Articles 5–9 primarily determined citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution. They should not be confused with the later statutory rules governing acquisition and termination of citizenship. The Citizenship Act, 1955 provides the principal legislative framework under Parliament's authority in Article 11.

Prelims focus

  • Citizenship provisions are contained in Part II, Articles 5–11.
  • Article 5: Domicile in India and specified birth or residence conditions.
  • Article 6: Migration from Pakistan to India.
  • Article 7: Migration from India to Pakistan after 1 March 1947.
  • Article 11: Parliament's power to regulate citizenship.
  • Trap: Article 5 is a provision concerning citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution, not the complete present-day citizenship procedure.

[Sources: Constitution of India, Part II, Articles 5–11; Citizenship Act, 1955; GCERT, Social Science, Standard 9, Chapter 8, Framing of Constitution and its Features, pp. 56–63. Consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Timeline shows the migration cut-offs under Articles 7 and 6, constitutional commencement on 26 January 1950, and the Citizenship Act, 1955.

title: Citizenship at the Commencement of the Constitution

body:
Three different questions about language

Language policy in India involves three related but different constitutional questions: which language is used for Union administration, which language or languages a State may use for its official work, and which languages receive recognition in the Eighth Schedule. These categories should not be treated as interchangeable.

Official language of the Union

Article 343 declares Hindi in the Devanagari script as the official language of the Union. It also specifies the international form of Indian numerals. The Constitution originally permitted the continued use of English for Union official purposes for 15 years from the commencement of the Constitution.

The Official Languages Act, 1963, particularly Section 3, provided for the continued use of English alongside Hindi for official purposes of the Union and parliamentary business. Its provisions were amended in 1967. Therefore, the expiry of the original 15-year period in 1965 did not result in the discontinuation of English.

India has no constitutionally declared national language

The Constitution identifies Hindi as the official language of the Union. It does not declare Hindi or any other language to be India's national language. English also continues to be used for Union official purposes under the Official Languages Act.

Official languages of the States

Article 345 empowers a State Legislature to adopt, by law, one or more languages in use in that State or Hindi as the official language or languages of the State. English shall continue to be used for those official purposes for which it was used immediately before the Constitution commenced, until the State Legislature provides otherwise by law.

Article 347 allows the President to direct recognition of a language spoken by a substantial proportion of a State's population when, on a demand, the President is satisfied that a substantial proportion of the State's population desires such official recognition. This provision helps address linguistic demands within a State.

Languages in the Eighth Schedule

The Eighth Schedule originally contained 14 languages when the Constitution commenced. Subsequent constitutional amendments increased the number to 22 languages. The current list is:

  • Assamese
  • Bengali
  • Bodo
  • Dogri
  • Gujarati
  • Hindi
  • Kannada
  • Kashmiri
  • Konkani
  • Maithili
  • Malayalam
  • Manipuri
  • Marathi
  • Nepali
  • Odia
  • Punjabi
  • Sanskrit
  • Santhali
  • Sindhi
  • Tamil
  • Telugu
  • Urdu

The original 14 were Assamese, Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Kashmiri, Malayalam, Marathi, Oriya, Punjabi, Sanskrit, Tamil, Telugu and Urdu.

Important amendments to the Eighth Schedule

AmendmentYearChange
21st Amendment1967Sindhi added.
71st Amendment1992Konkani, Manipuri and Nepali added.
92nd Amendment2003Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali added; the amendment came into force in 2004.
96th Amendment2011Oriya renamed Odia.

Inclusion in the Eighth Schedule does not automatically make a language an official language of the Union or of every State. State official-language decisions are governed separately by Article 345.

Constitutional safeguards for linguistic minorities

  • Article 29(1): Any section of citizens having a distinct language, script or culture has the right to conserve it.
  • Article 30(1): Religious and linguistic minorities have the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice.
  • Article 350: A person may submit a representation for redress of a grievance in any language used in the Union or the State concerned.
  • Article 350A: Every State and local authority should endeavour to provide adequate facilities for instruction in the mother tongue at the primary stage for children belonging to linguistic minority groups. The President may issue directions for this purpose.
  • Article 350B: The President appoints a Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities. The officer investigates matters relating to constitutional safeguards for linguistic minorities and reports to the President. The President places the reports before Parliament and sends them to the concerned State Governments.
  • Article 351: The Union is directed to promote the spread and development of Hindi while drawing upon Hindustani and other Indian languages.

Prelims focus

  • Article 343: Hindi in Devanagari script is the official language of the Union.
  • Article 345: State official languages.
  • The Official Languages Act, 1963 provides for continued use of English.
  • The Eighth Schedule originally contained 14 languages and now contains 22.
  • Articles 350A and 350B protect linguistic minorities.
  • Trap: Scheduled languages, Union official language and State official languages are three different constitutional categories.

[Sources: Constitution of India, Part III, Articles 29–30; Part XVII, Articles 343–351; Eighth Schedule; Official Languages Act, 1963, Section 3, as amended in 1967; Constitution (21st, 71st, 92nd and 96th Amendment) Acts; GCERT, Social Science, Standard 9, Chapter 8, Framing of Constitution and its Features. Consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Union and State official languages are distinct from Eighth Schedule recognition; linguistic minority safeguards are separate constitutional protections.
